corpus.text: The five-state process model describes the life cycle of a process as New, Ready, Running, Waiting and Terminated. A process is admitted into the New state when it is created, moves to Ready when the scheduler dispatches it, enters Running when a processor is assigned, enters Waiting when it blocks on an event such as input output, and finally reaches Terminated when it completes or is aborted by the operating system.

The process control block is the kernel data structure that stores everything the operating system needs in order to manage a process. It holds the process identifier, the program counter and processor register state, the scheduling priority, the memory management page table pointer, the accounting information and the list of open files and sockets owned by the process.

A deadlock requires four necessary conditions to hold simultaneously: mutual exclusion, in which a resource is held by at most one process; hold and wait, in which a process holds a resource while waiting for further resources; the absence of preemption, in which a granted resource cannot be forcibly removed; and circular wait, in which a cycle of waiting processes exists.

The banker's algorithm is a deadlock avoidance technique that grants a resource request only when the resulting allocation state remains safe. The algorithm simulates every possible completion order after the grant and proceeds only if at least one safe sequence exists, otherwise the request is deferred until later.

Page replacement algorithms decide which resident page to evict when a page fault occurs and no free frame remains. Least recently used tracks temporal locality and performs well on most workloads, first in first out is cheap but ignores future use, optimal replacement has the lowest fault rate but is unimplementable, and random provides no locality at all.

Handling a page fault is a fixed sequence of hardware and operating system steps. The memory management unit raises the fault trap, the operating system validates the reference, consults the free frame list or a page replacement policy, schedules the required disk read to bring the page into a frame, updates the page table, and finally restarts the instruction that caused the fault.

Disk scheduling determines the order in which queued block requests are served. First come first served is fair but suffers a long seek head movement, shortest seek time first reduces total movement but can starve distant requests, and the scan or elevator policy services requests in both directions while the head sweeps across the platter.

Memory allocation schemes trade internal and external fragmentation against one another. Contiguous allocation is simple and supports register addressing but suffers external fragmentation, fixed partitions waste memory internally, and paging eliminates external fragmentation at the cost of internal fragmentation within each fixed size page frame.

Round robin preemptive scheduling gives each ready process a fixed time slice on the processor and preempts it when the slice expires, handing the processor to the next process in the ready queue. Contrast this with non preemptive first come first served, where a long process at the head of the queue produces the convoy effect and delays every short process behind it.

A counting semaphore is a synchronisation primitive that holds a counter representing the number of available resource units. A process that needs the resource performs a wait operation that decrements the counter, blocking while the counter is zero, and releases it with a signal operation that increments the counter and wakes a blocked process, thereby coordinating access to a shared resource.

Virtual memory allows a process to address more memory than it physically owns by mapping virtual addresses onto frames. Address translation splits a virtual address into a page number and an offset, looks the page number up in the page table to obtain a frame number, and concatenates the frame number with the offset to form the physical address.

In retail banking, a banker's algorithm is sometimes used informally when describing a cash management heuristic for a branch that keeps a running reserve allocation. The branch planner reviews the pending withdrawal requests and the remaining reserve, allocates a safe portion of the reserve to each request, and defers the remainder when the allocation would fall below the required minimum balance.

Buffer allocation in a database engine decides which pages may remain resident in memory. A buffer pool holds a fixed number of frames, pages are allocated into free frames on first reference, an eviction policy chooses a victim page when no frame is free, and the dirty page is written back to storage before its frame is reused by another page.

Filler distractor. TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream over an unreliable packet network, using sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission timers and a sliding congestion window to keep the sender from overwhelming the receiver.

Filler distractor. The domain name system maps human readable host names to address records, and recursive resolution walks the hierarchy from the root servers down to an authoritative name server before caching the answer with a time to live.

Filler distractor. A hash table stores key value pairs in buckets chosen by a hash function, keeping the expected constant time lookup while collisions are resolved by chaining entries in a list or by probing an alternative open address.

Filler distractor. A breadth first search explores a graph level by level using a queue, whereas depth first search follows a single branch as far as it can using a stack, and both visit every vertex reachable from the start.

Priority scheduling assigns each process a numeric priority and always dispatches the highest priority process that is ready to run. When several processes share the top priority the scheduler may use ageing, which periodically reduces a waiting process's effective priority so that it cannot wait forever.

A trap synchronously transfers control to the kernel when a processor instruction detects a condition such as a divide error, a missing address translation or a protection violation. Unlike an interrupt, a trap is caused by the instruction that is executing and the saved processor state always points back at that instruction.

A thread is the smallest unit of execution that the processor scheduler dispatches. Threads of one process share the address space, the open file table and the signal handlers of that process, but each thread keeps its own program counter, register set and stack, so a fault in one thread need not destroy the whole process.

Multilevel feedback queue scheduling keeps several ready queues at different priority levels. A process that consumes its whole time slice is demoted to a lower queue, while a process that blocks early stays at its current level, and a periodic priority boost returns long waiting processes to the top queue so that no process starves.

Belady's anomaly is the observation that adding frames to a memory system can increase the number of page faults a demand paging system suffers. It occurs for replacement policies that evict the page whose next use is furthest in the future, such as optimal replacement, and it shows that the fault rate is not a monotone function of the memory available.

Indexing a file system tree means walking every directory and inode, reading each node's block list, and recording where the blocks live so that a later lookup can seek directly. The traversal is expensive on cold storage because each directory read is a separate random access, so a large tree benefits from caching directory blocks and from sorting entries to make the access pattern sequential.

The producer consumer problem describes a fixed size buffer shared by two classes of thread. A producer appends an item to the buffer and signals that the buffer is not empty, while a consumer removes an item and signals that the buffer is not full, and each side must wait on the appropriate condition variable when the buffer is in the wrong state rather than spinning.

A system call is the controlled entry point through which a user program asks the kernel for a service that only the kernel can provide, such as opening a file or mapping memory. The library wrapper places the requested service number and arguments in registers, executes a trap instruction to transfer control to the kernel, and returns the result to the caller on completion.

A superscalar processor issues several independent instructions per clock cycle from a single instruction stream, and a pipeline overlaps the fetch, decode, execute, memory and write back stages of successive instructions. To keep the stages busy the compiler reorders independent instructions, because a data dependency between two instructions stalls the pipeline regardless of how much execution width the processor has.

A branch predictor guesses the outcome of a conditional jump and speculatively fetches along the guessed path so that the pipeline is not flushed. A mispredicted branch costs the work already done on the wrong path, so processors use a branch target buffer and a history based predictor, and the cost grows with the depth of the speculation.

A write ahead log records every modifying operation in a durable sequential log before the change is applied to the main data structures, so that a crash can be recovered by replaying the log and undoing operations that were never committed. The log is the single serialisation point for concurrent transactions, which is what lets a database guarantee atomicity without locking the whole database.

Virtual memory isolation gives each process its own address space so that one process cannot read or write another's memory, and the memory management unit enforces the boundary on every load and store using the page table permissions. A page fault raised by a protection violation is delivered to the offending process as a fault signal, which the kernel may turn into a segmentation fault and terminate the process.

A cache sits between the processor and main memory to exploit temporal and spatial locality, and is organised into sets of lines indexed over part of the address. A direct mapped cache holds one possible line per set, a set associative cache holds several and checks them in parallel, and a write through cache updates memory on every store whereas a write back cache updates memory only when the line is evicted.

A training set is a fixed collection of labelled examples that the optimiser repeatedly reads while it adjusts the model parameters. A validation set is held out from training and used only to choose hyper parameters, and a test set is held out from both and touched once at the end, because a model selected on the same data it is scored on reports a performance that does not generalise.

Regularisation constrains a model so that it does not fit the noise in the training set. Adding a penalty on the magnitude of the weights shrinks them toward zero, and early stopping halts training once the validation error stops improving, both of which trade a small increase in training error for a reduction in the gap between training and unseen data.

The learning rate sets how far the parameters move in response to the gradient of the loss at each step. Too large a step overshoots the minimum and the loss diverges, too small a step makes convergence impractically slow, and schedules such as decay or momentum change the rate over training to reach a good solution faster.

A confusion matrix tabulates how often a classifier assigns each class label, with the true class on one axis and the predicted class on the other. The cell for the correct class gives the true positives, the off diagonal cells give the false positives and false negatives, and precision and recall are derived from those three counts rather than from the accuracy alone.

Deadlock. See deadlock conditions, deadlock detection, deadlock avoidance, deadlock prevention, deadlock resolution, deadlock cycle, resource allocation graph, Coffman conditions, hold and wait, circular wait, mutual exclusion, preemption, starvation versus deadlock, livelock, and the difference between them.

Portability of operating system abstractions across vendors. The buffer pool of a relational engine, the buffer cache of a file system, the page cache of a kernel, the cache of a processor and the process scheduling queue of a general purpose kernel are all called a buffer, a cache or a queue in different manuals, and the same word names different objects in each. Reading a manual for the wrong kernel therefore produces confident answers about the wrong mechanism.

Time sharing came to universities in the nineteen sixties, when a single processor had to serve a roomful of students who each believed the machine belonged to them. The economics mattered as much as the engineering: a processor that sat idle while one user composed a punch card was expensive, and a room in which a hundred users waited for a machine that was busy was worse. The compromise was to give each user a time slice on the processor and to preempt a running process when its slice ended, so that the queue of waiting processes moved and everyone got a turn. Advertisements for the arrangement led to the first time sharing operating systems.

The etymology of the term operating system runs from nineteenth century punch card tabulating machinery through the twentieth century batch job office, where a computer operator submitted a deck of punched cards, the processor read the jobs in strict submission order, and the operator queued each job behind the last. Commercial systems of that era offered no processor sharing, no time slice and no preemptive queue, so a single long job occupied the machine until it finished and every other job waited its turn. Operators learned to submit short jobs first, and the phrase operating system entered professional vocabulary long before the concept it now names.

Deadlock. Mutual exclusion. Hold and wait. No preemption. Circular wait. Exam revision sheet, week six.
